title: Reform, again
tomorrow: who calls God 'master' after escaping real masters?

cards: The season's over, the locker room is quiet, and someone finally says it: same thing next year? Every team, every family, every church hits that moment. Here's one.
A woman from Siena named Catherine, with no office and no title, is sending letter after letter to the pope. He's living in Avignon, in France, far from Rome. She calls him her sweet Christ on earth.
Then she tells him, plainly, to come back and be the shepherd he's meant to be. Who writes to a pope like that?

teach.h: SHE DIDN'T LEAVE. SHE CALLED IT BACK.
teach.b: Catherine did, and tradition remembers that the pope went back to Rome. Notice what she didn't do. She didn't leave, and she didn't burn it down.
She loved the Church enough to call it back to its own shape. That's what reform means here.

teach.h: BE REFORMED IN THE NEWNESS OF YOUR MIND.
teach.b: Paul uses the word in his letter to the Romans, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "be not conformed to this world; but be reformed in the newness of your mind." Re-formed: given back your form.
The Second Vatican Council said something like it about the Church itself. One document calls the Church holy and, at the same time, always in need of being purified.
Another speaks of Christ calling the Church to continual reformation while it's still on the road.
So two things are true at once: holy, and never finished.
Here's the one to tell a friend: Catherine's letters still exist, and she wrote to popes and kings and ordinary people with the same frankness. Reform didn't start with a council for her.
It started with one woman who loved the Church too much to stay quiet about it.
And the word reaches past the Church. Paul wasn't writing to buildings. He was writing to people, about minds that keep getting made new.

how: Catholics speak of the Church as holy and always in need of purification; renewal is sought through confession, the councils, and saints like Catherine of Siena, whom the Church names a Doctor of the Church.

o: replacing an old institution with a new one
a punishment that teaches someone to behave
giving something back its true shape, from within

games.q: reform, the Catholic way — tap the pairs.
p: wrote to the pope: come back
be reformed in the newness of your mind
holy, and always in need of purifying
the old thing given back its form

s: Catholic reform means starting a new church
in Catholic use it means calling the same Church back to its own shape, as Catherine did.
Vatican II described the Church as always in need of being purified
holy, and at the same time always in need of purification.
Catherine held an office that let her command the pope
she had no office or title. she wrote letters, frankly, out of love.

games.q: you're Catherine. you love the Church, and its leader is far from where he belongs. what do you do?
o: write to him plainly, with love: come back.
leave and start a community of your own.
stay quiet; it isn't your place to speak.
games.why: she kept writing, frankly and warmly, calling him her sweet Christ on earth and telling him to return. tradition remembers that he did.

practice: Pick one thing in your life that has slowly lost its shape: a habit, a friendship, a way you pray. Name what it would look like renewed, the one thing in the way, and the smallest first step.
If you pray, you can offer that step with Paul's line, be reformed in the newness of your mind.

wordCard.voice: Reform. To give something back its form: not a new thing, the old thing made new again.

orig.note: Latin, Romans 12:2 in the Vulgate: be reformed. the root of the English word reform.

carryVoice: Keep this: always renewing, holy and never finished, the way Catherine loved her Church. See you tomorrow.
